articles.title: Finding Duplicate Vitest Tests Without Running Them: What's New in VitestDedup
articles.excerpt: On the Tailwind CSS checkout I measured, VitestDedup 0.11.0 made 3,721 test registrations available for comparison, up from 2,169 in 0.10.0. That's a 71.6% increase, with the new analysis taking 1.74…
articles.body: On the Tailwind CSS checkout I measured, VitestDedup 0.11.0 made 3,721 test registrations available for comparison, up from 2,169 in 0.10.0. That's a 71.6% increase , with the new analysis taking 1.74 seconds. I maintain VitestDedup , a static analyzer that finds duplicate Vitest tests and opportunities to replace repeated test code with parameterized cases. Its main use case is an existing suite that has accumulated years of helpers, copied regressions, and different testing conventions. The goal is to process large amounts of test code quickly. VitestDedup reads source and configuration without executing them, so an initial maintenance review can start from a source checkout.
articles.author: Luiz Figueiredo

articles.title: How to tell whether a new favicon is actually live (or just a cached old one)
articles.excerpt: You replaced the favicon files, refreshed the site, and the old icon is still in the tab. This happens often enough that people assume the generator failed, or that their HTML is wrong, when the new p…
articles.body: You replaced the favicon files, refreshed the site, and the old icon is still in the tab. This happens often enough that people assume the generator failed, or that their HTML is wrong, when the new package is already on the server. Browsers, operating systems and even Google Search cache favicons aggressively. A hard refresh of the page is not always enough. This is a how-to for checking that the new icon is really being served, and for forcing stubborn clients to pick it up. First confirm the files on the server are the new ones Before you blame the browser, open the icon URLs directly. Visit /favicon.ico , the PNG paths in your snippet, and the Apple touch icon URL. You should see the new mark, not the old one.
articles.author: favicon.now

articles.title: Give Your AI Agent an IP Lookup Tool With Function Calling
articles.excerpt: LLM function calling guides love a fake tool. OpenAI's function calling guide demos a horoscope function that promises you'll "befriend a baby otter." Anthropic's tool use overview hardcodes "15 degre…
articles.body: LLM function calling guides love a fake tool. OpenAI's function calling guide demos a horoscope function that promises you'll "befriend a baby otter." Anthropic's tool use overview hardcodes "15 degrees Celsius, partly cloudy." Fine for showing the loop. Useless for learning what breaks when the function behind the tool calls a real, metered API. This post builds an IP lookup tool an agent can call: a strict schema, input validation, error results the model can read, a response cut from 576 tokens to 84, a five-minute cache, and the same function wired into OpenAI's Responses API and Claude's Messages API. Python, about 250 lines across three files. TL;DR The model never calls your API. It returns a tool name and JSON arguments; your code runs the call and sends the result back.
articles.author: ABDULLAH AFZAL

articles.title: I audited my own encrypted app and found the server could quietly strip the post-quantum half
articles.excerpt: I've been building Umbera for a while: messaging and calls without a phone number, with hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM encryption. I've written about the hybrid before. Under one of my posts someone pointed o…
articles.body: I've been building Umbera for a while: messaging and calls without a phone number, with hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM encryption. I've written about the hybrid before . Under one of my posts someone pointed out, fairly, that security claims you can't check aren't worth much. So this time I didn't ship features. I went through my own code the way an outside auditor would, someone paid to find the hole. I found more than I wanted to. Nothing leaked, and everything below is fixed and tested, shipping in the next app update. A couple of these stung, though. The post-quantum key nobody checked This is the worst one. Every message is sealed with two keys at once, classical X25519 and post-quantum ML-KEM-1024. The whole point of a hybrid is that you have to break both.
articles.author: Umbera

articles.title: Proofreader vs. Rewriter vs. Prompt API: Test the Task, Not the Demo
articles.excerpt: “Make this message better” is not one task. It can mean correcting a spelling mistake, changing the tone, shortening a paragraph, or clarifying an ambiguous commitment—and each version needs a differe…
articles.body: “Make this message better” is not one task. It can mean correcting a spelling mistake, changing the tone, shortening a paragraph, or clarifying an ambiguous commitment—and each version needs a different evaluation. That distinction matters when choosing Chrome’s writing APIs. The Proofreader API targets corrections. The Rewriter API changes expression, including tone and length. The Prompt API lets an application describe a task more generally. Comparing them requires a shared task definition, not just feeding each API the same sentence. This example uses two fair comparisons: proofreading against a constrained Prompt API baseline, and formal rewriting against a separate Prompt API baseline.
articles.author: Raju Dandigam

articles.title: Qwen3.5-27B on two NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti cards: 229k tokens of context
articles.excerpt: qwen3.5-27b holds 230k tokens of context and writes 24 tokens per second on a short prompt. Hand it a 100-page book and it starts answering after 20 s, then writes 4.5 times faster than you can read.…
articles.body: qwen3.5-27b holds 230k tokens of context and writes 24 tokens per second on a short prompt. Hand it a 100-page book and it starts answering after 20 s, then writes 4.5 times faster than you can read. It is a dense AI model with 27 billion parameters, a size that starts to be useful for analysis and general knowledge. Here, it runs on a computer with two NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti cards working together. Straight to the Results Qwen3.5-27b is usable on a computer with two NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti cards, but waits become very long at maximum context. Speed: 24 tokens per second on a short prompt, falling to 13 tokens per second at the full 229k-token context. Waiting: first word arrives in 541 ms on a short prompt and after 20 s on a 32k-token prompt.

But analyzing them takes forever, and you always feel like you are missing something important. This manifests in the typical scenario below: Interview 10-15 users (because that’s all you can realistically analyze) Spend days reading transcripts and looking for patterns, commonalities or themes You up with obvious insights everyone already suspected Team ends up making decisions based on incomplete data But, what if there was a better way? articles.body: While you were perfecting your user stories last week, GPT-4 wrote 50 of them in 3 minutes. And they were better than yours. I'm not trying to scare you. You know what, that's a lie. I am trying to scare you. Because what's coming for product management is bigger and faster than most PMs realize, and the window to adapt is closing rapidly. Something happened when I tested this myself: I fed Claude the same product requirements I'd spent 2 hours turning into user stories. articles.body: An image of Tharsis Tholus, a volcano on the surface of Mars, produced by ESA's Mars Express orbiter. (Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) Researchers have spotted an ancient, "dead" Martian volcano from orbit around the Red Planet. What is it? The European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, which has been orbiting and studying the planet since it arrived in 2003, recently captured incredible new imagery of the volcano Tharsis Tholus. This snapshot was captured by the spacecraft's High Resolution Stereo Camera. Even as old and worn as it is, the Martian volcano stands at around 4.97 miles (8 kilometers) tall which is comparable to some of the highest peaks in the Himalayan mountains.

articles.title: What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?
articles.excerpt: Conspiracy theories surround the odd-looking appearance of a shadow seen in the final images captured by Phobos 2, the Soviet Union’s last mission into deep space.
articles.body: On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service. However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft.
